title: Your data would disappear
explanation: {hosting} doesn't give your app a permanent disk, and {database} keeps data in a file on that disk. Anything people save would be lost on the next deploy or restart.
fix: Pick a hosted database, like Supabase, Neon or Turso, or a host with a permanent disk.
builder: Do not store app data in files on the server. Use the hosted database for everything people save.

title: Only works with a paid disk
explanation: {database} keeps data in a file, so {hosting} needs a paid permanent disk attached. Without it, the data is wiped on every redeploy.
fix: Attach a disk on {hosting} before launch, or switch to a hosted database.
builder: Store the database file only on the attached persistent disk path.

title: {hosting} can't run {framework}
explanation: {hosting} doesn't support {framework}, so your app would not run there.
fix: Pick a host that supports {framework}.

title: {framework} needs extra setup on {hosting}
explanation: {hosting} runs {framework} through an adapter or with some features missing. Expect extra setup and check which features work.
fix: Follow {hosting}'s official guide for {framework}, or pick a host with full support.
builder: Follow {hosting}'s official deployment guide for {framework}; some server features may not be available.

title: Nothing can push live updates
explanation: You want changes to show up instantly. {hosting} can't hold live connections open, and {database} has no live updates built in, so pages won't update without a refresh.
fix: Use a database with live updates built in, like Supabase or Firestore, or a host that holds live connections.
builder: Do not try to run a WebSocket server on {hosting}. Add a managed realtime service for live updates.

title: Live updates come from your database
explanation: {hosting} can't hold live connections, but {database} can push changes to browsers directly, so live updates still work.
builder: Use {database}'s built-in realtime feature for live updates. Do not run a WebSocket server on {hosting}.

title: Long jobs can get cut off
explanation: Requests on {hosting} have a time limit and it can't run background workers, so work that takes minutes can be stopped halfway.
fix: Pick a host with background workers, or add a background jobs service that can run long work.
builder: Never run long tasks inside a web request. Queue them and process them in the background.

title: No built-in way to run things on a schedule
explanation: {hosting} has no scheduled jobs, so daily emails or nightly cleanups need another service.
fix: Pick a host with scheduled jobs, or add a background jobs service that runs on a schedule.

title: Your payment keys need a server
explanation: {framework} apps run only in the browser, and anyone can read what's in the browser. Payment secret keys must live on a server.
fix: Pick a framework with server code, like Next.js or SvelteKit, or add server functions from your backend provider.
builder: Never put payment secret keys in client code. Create checkout sessions in server code.

title: Your AI key needs a server
explanation: {framework} apps run only in the browser, so an AI API key placed there can be copied and run up your bill.
fix: Pick a framework with server code, like Next.js or SvelteKit, or call the AI from a server function.
builder: Call the AI provider only from server code. Never expose the API key to the browser.

title: {hosting}'s free plan doesn't allow charging customers
explanation: You plan to take payments, and {hosting}'s free plan is for non-commercial projects. Budget for its paid plan from launch.
fix: Plan for {hosting}'s paid plan, or pick a host whose free plan allows commercial use.

title: Serverless code can run out of database connections
explanation: {hosting} starts many short-lived copies of your code, and each one opens its own connection to {database}. Busy moments can hit the connection limit.
fix: Use a database with pooling or an HTTP driver, like Neon or Supabase, or a host that keeps a server running.
builder: Use a pooled connection or serverless driver for {database}, and reuse one client per process.

title: {login} won't follow you to a phone app
explanation: You might build a phone app later, and {login} has no official mobile SDK, so you may have to switch login providers and move every account.
fix: Pick a login provider with a mobile SDK, like Supabase Auth, Clerk or Firebase Auth.

title: A phone app would reach {database} through your server
explanation: {database} has no official mobile SDK, so a future phone app would call your own server instead of the database directly. That's normal, just more work.

title: Big uploads will pass through your server
explanation: {files} can't take uploads straight from the browser, so large files travel through your server, where size and time limits can break them.
fix: Pick storage with direct uploads, like Supabase Storage, Cloudflare R2 or Amazon S3.
builder: Stream large uploads and enforce a maximum file size on the server.

title: Big uploads go straight to storage
explanation: {files} lets browsers upload directly, so large files skip your server and its size limits.
builder: Upload large files straight from the browser to {files} with signed upload URLs. Do not send them through server functions.

title: You handle sales tax
explanation: {payments} processes payments but isn't the legal seller, so sales tax and VAT are your job. A merchant of record, like Paddle, handles that for you.

title: Downloads cost money past the free amount
explanation: {files} charges when people download files beyond its free allowance, so popular images or videos can raise your bill.

title: AI costs money from the first request
explanation: {ai} has no free tier, so every request is billed. Set a monthly spending limit before you launch.
builder: Set usage limits per user and handle AI provider errors and rate limits gracefully.

title: {jobs} can't run long jobs on its own
explanation: {jobs} starts your jobs by calling your own app, so each job still has to finish inside your host's request time limit.
fix: Pick a jobs service that runs long work itself, or a host with background workers.
builder: Split long work into short steps that each finish well inside the host's request time limit.

title: Long jobs run in {jobs}
explanation: {jobs} can keep a job going for minutes or longer, so slow work doesn't have to fit inside a web request.
builder: Run anything slow as a {jobs} job, never inside a web request.

title: Nothing runs your scheduled tasks
explanation: Neither {hosting} nor {jobs} can run code on a schedule, so daily emails or nightly cleanups won't happen by themselves.
fix: Pick a jobs service or a host with scheduled runs.

title: Scheduled tasks run in {jobs}
explanation: {jobs} can start jobs on a schedule, like every morning, without a server that stays awake.
builder: Define scheduled tasks as {jobs} schedules, and make each run safe to repeat if it retries.

title: Login emails need an email service
explanation: {login} doesn't send sign-up and password-reset emails reliably enough for a launch on its own. Without an email service, people can get stuck unable to confirm their account.
fix: Add an email service in Email, then connect it as {login}'s email sender.

title: Login emails go through {email}
explanation: {login} can hand its sign-up and password-reset emails to {email}, which is built to deliver them.
builder: Configure {email} as {login}'s email sender (custom SMTP or its email hook) before launch.

title: Your email key needs a server
explanation: {framework} apps run only in the browser, so an email API key placed there can be copied and used to send spam from your domain.
fix: Pick a framework with server code, like Next.js or SvelteKit, or send email from a server function.
builder: Send email only from server code. Never expose the email API key to the browser.

title: Your phone app can't use {login} directly
explanation: {login} has no official mobile SDK, so signing in from the phone app means building that connection yourself or switching login providers.
fix: Pick a login provider with a mobile SDK, like Supabase Auth, Clerk or Firebase Auth.

title: Your phone app reaches {database} through your server
explanation: {database} has no official mobile SDK, so the phone app will call your own server, which then talks to the database.
builder: Give the phone app a small API on the server instead of database credentials. Phone apps can be unpacked, so never ship database keys inside one.

title: Your web and phone apps share React skills
explanation: {framework} and {mobile} both use React, so what you learn building one screen carries over to the other.

title: Two different ways of building screens
explanation: {framework} uses React and {mobile} doesn't, so the web app and the phone app are built with different tools and languages.

title: Two different ways of building screens
explanation: {mobile} uses React and {framework} doesn't, so the web app and the phone app are built with different tools.

title: Building the iPhone version needs a Mac
explanation: With {mobile}, building and publishing the iPhone app requires a Mac with Xcode. The Android version doesn't.

title: Publishing a phone app costs money
explanation: To publish on the App Store you join the Apple Developer Program for $99 a year, and Google Play charges a one-time $25 registration fee. These are separate from {mobile}.

title: Scraping needs server code
explanation: {framework} apps run only in the browser. Browsers won't let a page read other websites, and a scraping service's key placed there can be copied by anyone who opens your app.
fix: Pick a framework with server code, like Next.js or SvelteKit, and fetch pages from there.
builder: Fetch other websites only from server code or a background job, never from the browser.

title: {hosting} can't run scraping code
explanation: {hosting} only serves files and runs no server code, so there's nowhere to call {scraping} from or keep its key secret.
fix: Pick a host that runs server code.

title: {scraping} fits badly in {hosting}'s functions
explanation: {scraping} runs a real browser inside your own code. {hosting} runs short-lived functions with limits on size and run time that headless browsers often hit, so scrapes fail or time out.
fix: Run {scraping} on an always-on server host, or use a hosted scraper or hosted browser instead.
builder: Don't launch a headless browser inside a serverless or edge function.

title: Pages built with JavaScript cost more
explanation: {scraping} charges more to run a page's JavaScript, and many modern sites need it. Budget with the higher rate if your target sites fill in their content after loading.

title: {scraping} can't read pages built with JavaScript
explanation: Many sites fill in their pages with JavaScript after loading. {scraping} only sees the first HTML, so those pages come back empty.
fix: Check your target sites with JavaScript turned off, or pick a scraper that runs it.

title: Email needs a domain you own
explanation: Inbox providers check that email really comes from the domain it claims. Until you verify a domain of your own in {email}, messages to other people land in spam or can't be sent at all.
fix: Add a domain name, then add the DNS records {email} gives you to verify it.
builder: Send email only from an address on the app's own verified domain.

title: {hosting} charges to use your own domain
explanation: Connecting {domain}'s domain to {hosting} needs a paid plan, even if the rest of your app fits the free one.
fix: Budget for {hosting}'s paid plan, or pick a host that includes custom domains for free.

title: Free {hosting} apps fall asleep
explanation: On the free plan, {hosting} pauses your app after a while without visitors, and the next visitor waits while it starts again. Fine for testing; paid plans stay awake.

title: {analytics} sets cookies
explanation: In places with strict privacy laws, like the EU and UK, cookies used for analytics need visitors' consent first, so plan for a consent banner.
builder: Load analytics scripts that set cookies only after the visitor agrees.

title: Session replays can capture what people type
explanation: {monitoring} can record sessions to replay them. Mask form fields and personal details before turning replays on.
builder: Mask all form inputs and personal data in session replays.

title: {data_apis} can change or block you without warning
explanation: {data_apis} doesn't offer an official, supported API. The addresses your app reads can change shape or start refusing requests at any time, and its terms may not allow automated or commercial use.
fix: Cache what you fetch, keep showing the last good copy when a request fails, identify your app with a clear User-Agent, and read {data_apis}'s terms before you rely on it. For anything commercial, look for a licensed data source.
builder: Cache every response from {data_apis}, fall back to the last good copy on failure, and send a descriptive User-Agent.

title: Your {data_apis} key would be public
explanation: {framework} apps run only in the browser, and {data_apis} needs a key on every request. Anything in the browser can be read, so the key could be copied and used up on your account.
fix: Pick a framework with server code, or call {data_apis} from a server function and send only the results to the browser.
builder: Call {data_apis} only from server code and keep its key out of client bundles.
